I found several existing syntheses relevant to simulation for training and evaluating driving policies. Here is a draft literature review based on the syntheses without creating new ones:

---

### Literature Review: Simulation for Training and Evaluating Driving Policies

Simulation environments have become essential tools for the development, training, and evaluation of autonomous driving policies. A prominent theme across the literature is the use of mid-level representations and simulation platforms to improve autonomous driving research and deployment workflows.

#### Mid-Level Representations and Simulation Platforms

Papers highlight the advantage of mid-level input representations combined with simulation for autonomous driving. For example, ChauffeurNet, presented in one study, uses a recurrent neural network (RNN) that takes mid-level inputs and outputs driving trajectories. This architecture facilitates training on both real and simulated data and supports closed-loop simulation testing before real-world deployment, enhancing safety and flexibility (synthesis 3f129bca-07c9-5298-b172-3f5778edd0c9, synthesis ce7b1830-0eb7-5593-a9ac-93e8e7c4d4a0).

The CARLA simulator, an open-source urban driving environment described in another study, supports the development, training, and validation of autonomous urban driving systems. CARLA allows flexible sensor suite specifications, environmental condition variations, and provides detailed urban content such as vehicles and pedestrians. This simulator supports not only the training and prototyping of driving models but also their controlled evaluation and compliance measurement with traffic rules (synthesis fd4a75d1-185b-5799-a7f8-8760518029b6, synthesis 3f129bca-07c9-5298-b172-3f5778edd0c9).

#### End-to-End Learning Approaches in Simulation

In parallel with mid-level methods, end-to-end learning approaches have also been explored. One study presents a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the entire processing pipeline from raw camera images to steering commands. This end-to-end approach has been evaluated using the CARLA simulator as well, which supports different autonomous driving methodologies including imitation learning (synthesis a8f51cdd-aa56-57c2-9104-aa1ce1db15d6, synthesis fb724a87-5e78-5eb1-8f3d-e25b13d008ee).

#### Comparative Insights and Gaps in the Literature

Comparisons between these approaches reveal fundamental differences. The mid-level RNN approach outputs driving trajectories based on structured input, whereas the end-to-end CNN directly maps images to steering commands (synthesis cd99f152-7dcf-5e66-b117-d58014ff7622, synthesis 17a05dce-087e-5fc5-b168-f9978f85b590). Despite the detailed descriptions of both methods, there is a notable gap: no direct empirical comparison under the same conditions or datasets has been reported for these fundamentally different architectures. This limits understanding of their relative performance and suitability for specific autonomous driving tasks (synthesis 64b32c2a-bb5b-52a2-a778-829d9c303fa7, synthesis 4d5f18f5-d4a6-57dc-885a-fb6dc0331300).
